title: Board of Regents of State Colleges v. Roth (1972)
shortTitle: Board of Regents of State Colleges v. Roth (1972)
summary: A one-year appointment with no secured renewal interest did not give Roth a procedural entitlement to reasons and a hearing on nonrenewal.

sections.Parties: David Roth, a nontenured assistant professor at Wisconsin State University–Oshkosh, sued university officials after they declined to renew his appointment. The Board of Regents defended the applicable employment rules.
sections.Material Facts: Roth’s first appointment ran from September 1, 1968, to June 30, 1969. Wisconsin provided tenure only after the required period of year-to-year service and did not otherwise constrain renewal of his contract. Officials gave timely notice of nonretention but no reasons or hearing. Roth alleged both retaliation for criticism of university administrators and denial of procedural due process. The nonrenewal itself carried no charge of dishonesty or comparable stigma and did not exclude him from other employment.
sections.Procedural History: The district court accepted the procedural claim by balancing Roth’s interest in another appointment against the university’s interest in summary nonrenewal. The Supreme Court rejected that approach to the threshold question and held that the asserted liberty and property interests did not require a hearing in these circumstances. Marshall’s dissent is included; Douglas’s separate dissent is omitted.
sections.Issue: Did nonrenewal deprive Roth of liberty or property protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, so that officials had to state reasons and allow a hearing?
sections.Holding: On the circumstances described, Roth had no protected property interest in renewal and no demonstrated liberty deprivation from the simple loss of this job. Due process therefore did not require the requested hearing merely because continued employment mattered greatly to him.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority separated whether an interest is protected from how much process protects it. Importance and hardship help determine procedure after the threshold is met; they do not independently create a property right. A property claim must rest on an existing rule or understanding that secures the benefit. Roth’s appointment secured employment through its termination date and contained no renewal promise; no other statute, rule, or sufficiently established institutional practice supplied one.

Liberty could be implicated by a stigmatizing public charge or a restriction foreclosing other employment opportunities. The majority found neither in the record as described. A name-clearing hearing, when required, would permit rebuttal of the charge and would not itself guarantee rehiring. Marshall accepted the general framework but would define liberty and property more broadly to require government to give reasons for denying employment opportunities and act fairly. The procedural holding does not settle whether an otherwise discretionary employment choice violated the First Amendment.
